headline: Schools Transform Lunch Halls Into Teaching Spaces
meta_description: England's government overhauls school food standards for the first time in over a decade, banning deep-fried food and partnering with schools to teach children…
summary_short: Schools across England are reimagining lunch as an educational experience, teaching children to embrace healthier foods through tasting sessions and hands-on cooking.
body:
England's government is overhauling school food standards for the first time in more than a decade—a move that extends far beyond simply swapping chips for vegetables. Starting in September 2027, the new standards will ban deep-fried foods like chicken nuggets and chips, restrict high-sugar desserts to once weekly, and encourage pulses, grains, and vegetables across menus. But the real story isn't in the rules: it's in how schools are winning children over to these changes through education and taste. At Greenside primary school in west London, five-year-olds queue excitedly for chickpea and spicy rice burritos with roasted sweet potatoes and braised spinach. On Fridays, a "breaducation" programme lets pupils bake focaccia alongside their regular lessons, filling the lunch hall with the aroma of freshly baked bread. This integrated approach—where sustainability and food knowledge become part of the curriculum itself—is being replicated across the country.

The challenge, however, is genuine. Three-quarters of UK parents worry about what their children eat at school, and one in three primary school pupils leave overweight or obese. Many schools still serve bland, highly processed meals. The government's solution includes extending free school meals to 500,000 additional children, but experts stress that rules alone won't work. As food writer Bee Wilson notes, "It doesn't matter how healthy a lunch is if most of it goes in the bin." Her charity, TastEd, provides free food education resources to schools. At Christ's College in Finchley, north London, head chef Amber Francis runs a weekly "Try Something New Day" at breaktime, offering pupils tastings of unfamiliar ingredients like kohlrabi and pomelo to build their confidence with new flavours.

For the government's ambitious plans to succeed, schools must combine stricter standards with genuine food education—turning lunch halls into spaces where children learn that healthy eating isn't a sacrifice, but a discovery.
quick_facts: England's government bans deep-fried school foods starting September 2027
Greenside primary in west London serves chickpea burritos and student-baked bread
Three-quarters of UK parents concerned about school lunch nutrition
Christ's College runs weekly tasting sessions with unfamiliar vegetables
New standards reach 500,000 more children through free school meals expansion
